Basalt. The most abundant igneous rock on Earth, formed when low-silica lava cools rapidly at the surface. It makes up most of the oceanic crust and the floors of mid-ocean ridges, and it's rich in iron and magnesium, which gives it that characteristically dark colour and high density.

Basalt is mafic, meaning it's high in magnesium and iron, and low in silica—about fifty percent silicon dioxide. The rapid cooling of those lava flows produces fine grains or a glassy texture that you can't resolve with the naked eye. The primary minerals are plagioclase feldspar, which is calcium-rich, and pyroxene, an iron-magnesium silicate. Olivine is common in some basalts as well.

The colour ranges from dark grey to black because of all that iron and magnesium, and it's denser than granitic rocks—around three grams per cubic centimetre compared to two point seven. It can weather into fertile soil because iron and magnesium are plant nutrients, which is why volcanic regions with basaltic soils are often agriculturally rich. Historically, basalt has been used as construction aggregate, crushed for road base, and as whetstones and tool-making material.

Granite, by contrast, is felsic—light and silica-rich—while basalt is mafic and silica-poor. Together they represent opposite ends of the igneous rock spectrum. Basalt is the quintessential extrusive igneous rock made from lava, whereas granite is the intrusive equivalent. And under the right conditions of burial and heat, basalt can be metamorphosed to greenschist or amphibolite.
